title: Find Median from Data Stream
description: Two heaps: a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half, kept balanced. addNum O(log n), findMedian O(1).

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down the contract.
sections.say:
"Let me restate: I'm building a `MedianFinder` class with two ops — `addNum(n)` ingests a value from a stream, and `findMedian()` returns the median of every value seen so far. Both can be called in any interleaving, any number of times."

Then a few quick clarifying questions:
• Are the numbers integers, or could they be floats? (Affects whether the average for even counts needs special care.)
• Range — could n be astronomically large? Negative?
• Is `findMedian` called frequently relative to `addNum`, or vice versa? (Affects which side to optimize.)
• If no numbers have been added yet, what should `findMedian` return — 0, undefined, NaN, throw?
• Are we allowed O(n) memory for the running set, or is there a strict memory bound?
sections.why: The 'call frequency' question is the load-bearing one — it tells you whether to optimize addNum (sorted array: O(n) add, O(1) median) or findMedian (two heaps: O(log n) add, O(1) median) or strike a balance. The standard contract is 'both ops called often' which is why the two-heaps answer dominates. The empty-state question protects against an array-out-of-bounds crash on `findMedian()` before any `addNum` — easy to miss, easy to ask about up front.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the obvious approaches before reaching for two heaps.
sections.say:
"Two simple baselines.

"Version A: append to an unsorted array on add, sort on every findMedian. Add is O(1), but findMedian is O(n log n) — disastrous if findMedian is called often.

"Version B: maintain a sorted array. Each addNum does a binary search for the insert position (O(log n)) but the actual splice to make room is O(n). findMedian is O(1) — just read the middle element(s). So add is O(n), findMedian is O(1).

"Both are unacceptable if both ops fire millions of times. We need a structure where add is *log* and findMedian is constant."
sections.why: Running through both baselines explicitly is the move because it sets up the two-heap insight as a deliberate trade rather than a magic answer. Version A optimizes add at the cost of findMedian; Version B does the reverse. Two-heaps is the *Pareto improvement* — it makes add O(log n) instead of O(n), and keeps findMedian O(1). That's not a coincidence — it's exactly what a balanced-tree structure could give you, and the two-heap trick is the special case that's much simpler to implement than a balanced BST.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern
sections.prompt: Why two heaps, and why max + min specifically?
sections.say:
"Here's the insight: the median only depends on the *one or two middle elements*. I don't need the full sorted order — I just need fast access to the boundary between the lower half and the upper half. So I split the stream into two halves and keep each half in a heap:

• `lo` = max-heap holding the lower half. Root = largest of the smalls.
• `hi` = min-heap holding the upper half. Root = smallest of the bigs.

"The two roots together ARE the median candidates: if total count is odd, the median is the root of whichever heap is bigger; if even, it's the average of the two roots. Both are O(1) reads.

"To make this work I need two invariants. First, *partition correctness*: every value in `lo` ≤ every value in `hi`. Second, *balance*: `lo.size - hi.size ∈ {0, 1}` — they're equal, or `lo` has one extra (by convention). Both invariants are restored after every add by routing the new value to the correct heap, then transferring at most one element across the boundary.

"The reason it's max-heap on the *lower* side and min-heap on the *upper*: I always need the root of each heap to point INTO the boundary — the largest of the smalls and the smallest of the bigs. That's how the median falls out trivially. If I'd picked min-heap for lo and max-heap for hi, the roots would point AWAY from the boundary and I'd have to scan to find the median."
sections.why: Naming both invariants — partition correctness AND balance — is what proves you understand the algorithm rather than memorized it. The partition invariant is what makes the median computable from the roots; the balance invariant is what makes the *which root* decision O(1). The 'max for lower, min for upper, both pointing into the boundary' framing is the geometric intuition that makes this stick — once you see it as 'two heaps facing each other at the median line,' you never forget the heap-type choice.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few sequences to confirm both invariants are maintained.
sections.intro: "Let me trace through a few op sequences to confirm both invariants hold throughout." Three sequences — the canonical odd/even alternation, a longer sequence that exercises a transfer in both directions, and a sequence where values arrive in a bad order to stress the rebalance.

examples.note: Canonical small case — odd then even transitions.
examples.trace:
addNum(1): lo empty → lo.push(1). lo=[1], hi=[]. balance ok.
addNum(2): lo.peek=1, 2>1 → hi.push(2). lo=[1], hi=[2]. balance ok (lo=hi).
findMedian: lo.size=hi.size=1, even → (1+2)/2 = 1.5 ✓
addNum(3): lo.peek=1, 3>1 → hi.push(3). lo=[1], hi=[2,3]. hi.size=2 > lo.size=1 → transfer: lo.push(hi.pop()=2). lo=[2], hi=[3]. balance ok.
findMedian: lo.size=hi.size=1, even → (2+3)/2 = 2.5? — wait, expected 2.

Re-check: after addNum(3), counts are lo=[1], hi=[2,3]. The rebalance moves hi's smallest (2) to lo: lo=[2,1] (max-heap, root=2), hi=[3]. Now lo.size=2, hi.size=1 (odd total) — and lo.size > hi.size, so findMedian returns lo.peek()=2 ✓

examples.input: addNum(1), addNum(2), findMedian, addNum(3), findMedian, addNum(4), findMedian
examples.note: Longer sequence — exercises both transfer directions across the boundary.
examples.trace:
addNum(1): lo=[1], hi=[]
addNum(2): 2>lo.peek=1 → hi=[2]. balance ok.
findMedian: even (1,1) → (1+2)/2 = 1.5 ✓
addNum(3): 3>lo.peek=1 → hi=[2,3]. hi(2)>lo(1) → move hi.pop()=2 to lo. lo=[2,1] (max-heap, root=2), hi=[3]. lo larger by 1 ✓
findMedian: lo larger → lo.peek=2 ✓
addNum(4): 4>lo.peek=2 → hi=[3,4]. hi.size=lo.size, balance ok.
findMedian: equal sizes → (lo.peek=2 + hi.peek=3)/2 = 2.5 ✓

examples.input: addNum(5), addNum(1), addNum(3), findMedian, addNum(2), findMedian
examples.note: Adversarial order — values arrive in 5, 1, 3, 2 instead of sorted. Stress-tests routing and rebalance.
examples.trace:
addNum(5): lo empty → lo.push(5). lo=[5], hi=[].
addNum(1): lo.peek=5, 1<=5 → lo.push(1). lo=[5,1] (max-heap, root=5). lo larger by 2! transfer lo.pop()=5 → hi.push(5). lo=[1], hi=[5]. balance ok.
addNum(3): lo.peek=1, 3>1 → hi.push(3). lo=[1], hi=[3,5] (min-heap, root=3). hi(2)>lo(1) → move hi.pop()=3 to lo. lo=[3,1] (max-heap, root=3), hi=[5]. lo larger by 1.
findMedian: lo larger → lo.peek=3 ✓
addNum(2): lo.peek=3, 2<=3 → lo.push(2). lo=[3,1,2] (max-heap, root=3). lo.size=3 > hi.size+1=2! transfer lo.pop()=3 → hi.push(3). lo=[2,1] (max-heap, root=2), hi=[3,5]. balance ok.
findMedian: equal sizes → (lo.peek=2 + hi.peek=3)/2 = 2.5 ✓

sections.why: The first trace surfaces the easiest-to-get-wrong moment — after addNum(3) in the first example, a naive implementation that *only* routes by value (without rebalancing) leaves the heaps lopsided and gives the wrong median. The transfer-back-to-lo step is what restores the invariant. The third trace is the killer — it shows that the algorithm doesn't depend on input order at all, because the rebalance step is unconditional after every add. If you can trace a worst-case order without errors, the algorithm is correct.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Edges worth flagging:
• findMedian called before any addNum → both heaps empty, lo.peek() returns undefined, division NaN. Decide and document — typically throw or return null.
• Single addNum then findMedian → lo=[n], hi=[]. lo.size > hi.size, returns lo.peek() = n ✓.
• All identical values (1,1,1,1,1) → routing always lands in lo (n <= lo.peek()), but rebalance pumps half over to hi. The invariant holds; median is always 1.
• Two-value heaps with equal peeks → routing tie-breaks by `<=` going to lo, which is a deliberate choice — preserves the 'lo larger or equal' convention.
• Integer median with even count → result is a float (.5). Make sure the contract allows that; some specs ask for floor or rounding.
• Very long stream → memory is O(n) and unavoidable for the exact-median problem. If memory is bounded, the interviewer is probably hinting at approximate-median algorithms (reservoir sampling, P² estimator, t-digest) — worth flagging."
sections.why: The 'memory grows with n' callout is the senior-tier signal — most candidates implement the two-heap solution without realizing that exact streaming median is fundamentally Ω(n) memory. The moment the interviewer asks 'what if the stream is too big to hold in memory?' you pivot to approximate algorithms (P², t-digest), which is a whole different family of techniques. Mentioning that family unprompted shows you know where this problem sits in the broader space.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity claim?
sections.say:
"addNum is O(log n) — one heap push (O(log n)), at most one transfer (one pop + one push, each O(log n)) — so 3 log n total in the worst case, dropping the constant.

"findMedian is O(1) — just read one or two roots and possibly average them.

"Space is O(n) — both heaps together hold every value seen. Unavoidable for exact-median; bounded-memory variants accept approximation error.

"If you wanted to extend this: a 'sliding-window median' (median of the last k values, not all values) keeps the same two-heap shape but adds a 'lazy delete' or sorted-multiset structure to remove the value falling out of the window. The two-heap template is preserved; what changes is the bookkeeping for removals. Bigger jump: 'k-th quantile of a stream' (not just median) generalizes to k+1 heaps with the boundary shifted, or to dedicated quantile sketches like t-digest if approximation is OK."
sections.why: The amortization defense here is the cleanest part of the algorithm — addNum does at most 3 heap operations, each O(log n), with no nested loops or hidden costs. The bonus material — sliding-window median, t-digest — proves you see this as a *prototype* for the broader class of streaming-statistics problems. Naming t-digest unprompted shows you've worked at the boundary between exact and approximate algorithms, which is the staff-level signal. The 'k+1 heaps for k-th quantile' generalization is the move that turns the two-heap trick into a transferable pattern.

reference.approach: Two heaps — max-heap low half, min-heap high half
notes: Invariant: every value in `lo` is <= every value in `hi`, and `lo.size() - hi.size()` is 0 or 1.
Route incoming n by comparing to `lo.peek()`; then rebalance by transferring at most one element.
If total count is odd, `lo` holds the extra and `lo.peek()` is the median. If even, average the two roots.
reference.crux: Split the stream into a max-heap (lower half) and min-heap (upper half) facing the median line, kept balanced — the median is always one or both roots, read in O(1).
cruxDistractors: Keep one sorted array; binary-search the insert spot on each add and read the middle element — but the splice makes add O(n).
Use a min-heap for the lower half and a max-heap for the upper half so each root points away from the boundary.
Maintain a single min-heap of all values and pop n/2 elements on each findMedian to reach the middle one.

alternates.label: Sorted array (binary-search insert)
alternates.when: Use when addNum is called rarely but findMedian is called constantly — the sorted invariant gives O(1) median reads. The O(n) splice cost is only paid on insert, not on every findMedian call. Also a good starting point in an interview before presenting the heap optimization.
alternates.complexity: O(n) add / O(1) median / O(n) space
notes: Binary search finds the index in O(log n) but splice must shift all subsequent elements — the insert is O(n) even with the fast lookup.
findMedian is O(1): just index into the middle of the sorted array (two reads for even count).
This is the natural 'step 2' answer — start here to show you understand the problem, then motivate two-heaps as the O(log n) add upgrade.

questions.q: Why use a MAX-heap for the lower half and a MIN-heap for the upper half?
options: So both heaps share the same comparator, allowing the rebalance step to swap roots without a sign flip
So the two heap roots are the median candidates
A max-heap on the upper half would route incoming values incorrectly because hi.peek() would be the maximum, not the minimum
Inverting the types lets `lo.size - hi.size` stay non-negative without an explicit rebalance
questions.explain: The median sits on the boundary between the two halves, so you need the largest of the lows and the smallest of the highs — `lo.peek()` and `hi.peek()` are exactly those, which is what makes `findMedian` O(1).
One push, then at most one rebalance transfer (a pop plus a push) — every heap operation costs O(log n).
It only reads `lo.peek()` / `hi.peek()` plus a size comparison; all the ordering work was already paid for inside `addNum`.

questions.q: When the two heaps have equal size, the median is:
options: lo.peek() — by the convention that lo holds the lower-or-equal half
hi.peek() — the smaller of the two valid medians for an even count
Either peek — they are equal whenever the heaps are balanced
questions.explain: Equal sizes means an even total, so the two middle values ARE the two roots and the median is their average; `lo.peek()` alone is the answer only when `lo` is the larger heap (odd total).
